title: Seeing God (ST I-II.3.8)
hookLine: final happiness is seeing God's essence

cards: A small child in the back seat asks why the sky is blue. You answer with sunlight. "Why?"
You try something about air. "Why?" A few whys later every adult in the car is out of answers, and the child is still going.
Thomas Aquinas treats it as a clue. On his account, that little engine of why doesn't switch off in adults. It just gets quieter, buried under errands.
Today he says what the will's long hunger is actually for. Seeing God.

teach.b: Thomas starts with wonder. When we see an effect and know it has a cause, we want to know what that cause is, and the wanting doesn't rest until it gets an answer. Follow it up through every cause, and you arrive at God.

teach.h: KNOWING THAT GOD IS: NOT ENOUGH.
teach.b: Knowing that God exists isn't enough. The arguments from last week can show there is a first cause. They can't show what God is.
And a mind that knows only that, Thomas says, is still asking.
So final happiness, for Thomas, can only be one thing: the mind seeing God's very essence, what God is. Not an idea about God. God, seen.
The tradition calls it the beatific vision, the seeing that makes blessed. Jesus, in the Douay-Rheims: "Blessed are the clean of heart: for they shall see God."

Paul: "We see now through a glass in a dark manner; but then face to face." And the First Letter of John: "we shall be like to him: because we shall see him as he is." Thomas is honest that this life doesn't deliver it.

teach.h: PARTIAL HERE, FULL AS A GIFT.
teach.b: Here, happiness is real but partial.

The full thing is a gift, not an achievement. So if an ordinary week leaves a restlessness behind, on Thomas's account it isn't a defect. It's the shape of a person made for something no errand can supply.
The child in the back seat is onto something.

how: Catholics hope for the beatific vision, seeing God face to face, as the final happiness of the saints, and the Church's prayers for the dead and its feast of All Saints speak of this hope.

o: a dream or vision seen during prayer
knowing for sure that God exists
the mind beholding what God is, face to face

p: not enough to rest the mind

s: for Thomas, proving that God exists is final happiness
knowing that God is still leaves the mind asking what God is. only seeing God's essence rests it.
Thomas says perfect happiness isn't reached in this life
here it's real but partial. the full vision is a gift.
for Thomas, wonder is a childish thing we should outgrow
he starts his argument with wonder: the desire to know the cause doesn't rest until it reaches God.

games.q: you're Thomas. you've ruled out money, fame, power and pleasure. a student asks: then what is happiness? what do you answer?
o: the mind seeing what God is, face to face.
feeling peaceful most of the time.
games.why: Thomas says final happiness is the vision of God's essence. knowing only that God exists leaves wonder still asking.

practice: Let one big why you carry come up, not a practical one: why is there anything, why do I love the people I love, why does beauty hurt a little?

Don't answer it; let it stay open the way a child's why stays open, and notice the pull of wanting to know, which Thomas would say is pointing somewhere. If you pray, say the line from Matthew: they shall see God.

wordCard.voice: Seeing God. For Thomas, final happiness is the mind seeing God's essence, face to face, the vision the tradition calls beatific. Today's word.

orig.note: Latin, the language Thomas wrote in: the vision of the divine essence.

carryVoice: Your line: made to see him. A small restlessness isn't a defect; it points past every errand. See you tomorrow.
